newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia on edge as Yeltsin surgery starts.
newsitem.headline: Russia on edge as Yeltsin surgery starts.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin entered the operating theatre at 7 a.m. (0400 GMT) on Tuesday for a heart bypass operation that aims to restore him to the Kremlin after months in which Russia has looked dangerously leaderless.

The 65-year-old leader's last act before going under the anaesthetic was to hand over power, including Russia's nuclear trigger, to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, one of the figures manoeuvring for position around the sick president.
According to a plan announced in advance in a new display of Kremlin openness, a second decree will return power to Yeltsin shortly after the president regains consciousness.
Chernomyrdin, 58, and a possible successor, has effectively been running the country since Yeltsin's re-election on July 3.

As Yeltsin went under the surgeon's knife, thousands marched in Russia's Far East in strikes and demonstrations called by trade unions to protest against unpaid wages -- the most potent symbol of the country's massive economic problems.
U.S. President Bill Clinton, who faces reelection on Tuesday, sent Yeltsin "best wishes for a speedy recovery".
Western leaders see Yeltsin, who led Russia out of communism in 1991, as the guarantor of Russia's shaky democracy and fear his loss could plunge it into a period of deeper instability.

Doctors have said the widely expected operation would last six to eight hours. It is a common procedure to improve the blood supply to Yeltsin's heart by grafting in veins to divert blood around three or four blockages in his cardiac arteries.

It was being performed by Russian surgeon Renat Akchurin, 50, who previously performed a bypass on Chernomyrdin. Michael DeBakey, the 88-year-old U.S. cardiologist who pioneered the bypass technique more than 30 years ago, was advising him.
Hundreds of bypass operations are performed around the world every day. Only some two percent fail.
Medical experts say the biggest risk to the president may be problems with other organs, like his liver. Two German doctors specialised in post-operative complications are on hand.

Presidential spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky confirmed the operation had begun after journalists saw a motorcade including Yeltsin's Mercedes limousine sweep into the Cardiology Research Centre in leafy suburban Moscow before dawn.
The president had been staying at the nearby Barvikha state sanatorium while preparing for surgery, which he announced on television in a moment of unprecedented candour on September 5.
That ended weeks of equivocation by aides who had been explaining Yeltsin's absence since before his reelection on July 3 by saying he had a cold and various other minor ailments.
The admission that the president, who had two heart attacks last year, needed major surgery also fueled a bitter struggle for influence in the Kremlin.

It involved notably Chernomyrdin, chief of the presidential staff Anatoly Chubais and General Alexander Lebed, a political maverick roped in to the Kremlin in June to help Yeltsin secure victory over his communist rival in the July 3 election.
Yeltsin finally sacked Lebed on October 17 amid a flurry of accusations and counter-accusations of mysterious plots and plans to seize power.
The 46-year-old paratrooper remains a key political figure and polls show he would be a strong contender for the presidency if Yeltsin were forced to step down.
If that were to happen Chernomyrdin would rule in the interim with a mandate to hold an election within three months.

Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, 52, would also be a challenger in a new vote. He complained the Kremlin cheated to beat him in July by concealing that Yeltsin had had a suspected third heart attack. Yeltsin beat Zyuganov by 13 points.
